evals.name: shape-a-pitch-from-scratch
evals.prompt: I'm a PM at a B2B SaaS (~40 people, post-PMF, ~$8M ARR). Our biggest customer complaint is that our reporting dashboard is confusing. Leadership just said 'let's redesign the reporting dashboard.' Help me shape this bet using Ryan Singer's Shape Up method.
evals.expected_output: Output should: (a) push back on jumping to shaping — 'improve the dashboard' or 'redesign it' is an unframed problem; force framing first (whose problem, why now, business value); (b) reference Singer's 2022 Framing essay explicitly; (c) walk through the five ingredients of a Package once framing is done (Problem, Appetite, Solution, Rabbit Holes, No-Gos); (d) insist on setting Appetite BEFORE designing the Solution — appetite is a design constraint, not a prediction; (e) mention fat marker sketches / breadboarding as the fidelity level for the Solution; (f) cite Singer at least once with a specific source (book chapter URL, essay URL, or podcast); (g) NOT jump straight to designing screens or handing over a task breakdown; (h) reference the 2025 gym-management case study as a similar pattern (vague ask → SME conversation → sharper framed problem).
assertions: Output pushes back on 'redesign the dashboard' as an unframed problem before shaping
Output cites Singer's Framing (2022) essay or the framing → shaping distinction
Output walks through all five ingredients (Problem, Appetite, Solution, Rabbit Holes, No-Gos)
Output insists on setting Appetite BEFORE the Solution
Output mentions fat marker sketches OR breadboarding as the fidelity level
Output cites at least one specific Singer source (book chapter URL, essay URL, or podcast episode)
Output does NOT jump to designing screens or a task breakdown
Output uses 'Package' or 'Pitch' correctly (not 'PRD', 'user story', or 'requirements doc')

evals.name: critique-a-doc-that-is-really-a-scrum-backlog-item
evals.prompt:
Please critique this pitch I wrote against the Shape Up method.

---

PITCH: Reporting Dashboard v2

As a customer, I want a better reporting dashboard so that I can understand my data.

Acceptance criteria:
- Faster load times (target: <2s)
- More charts (target: 8+ chart types)
- Export to Excel
- Mobile-responsive
- Dark mode

Estimated: 34 story points (~3 sprints)

Priority: P0

Dependencies: blocked on Analytics API v3 (currently in backlog)

---

Review this against Ryan Singer's Shape Up.
evals.expected_output: Output should identify that this is NOT a Shape Up pitch — it's a user story + acceptance criteria in Scrum format with story-point estimation. Specifically it should: (a) name that this uses user-story-as-pitch which is not the Shape Up shape; (b) name the missing five ingredients (specifically: no specific-story Problem, no Appetite (it uses story points instead), no Solution at fat-marker fidelity (just a feature list), no Rabbit Holes, no No-Gos); (c) call out story points as estimation, not appetite — the two are not interchangeable; (d) call out 'blocked on backlog' as a Shape Up anti-pattern (no backlog); (e) cite Singer specifically — Ch. 6 Write the Pitch or Ch. 7 Bets Not Backlogs; (f) suggest what a real Shape Up pitch/package would look like for this same customer problem.
assertions: Output identifies this as a user-story-and-acceptance-criteria doc rather than a Shape Up pitch
Output names at least 3 of the 5 missing ingredients (Problem-as-specific-story, Appetite, Solution-at-fat-marker-fidelity, Rabbit Holes, No-Gos)
Output challenges the use of story-point estimation as inconsistent with Shape Up's appetite discipline
Output challenges the reference to 'blocked on backlog' as inconsistent with Shape Up's no-backlog stance
Output cites Bill's book at least once — specifically Ch. 6 (Write the Pitch), Ch. 7 (Bets Not Backlogs), or a related URL
Output does NOT just accept the pitch and offer polish suggestions
Output distinguishes appetite (fixed time, variable scope) from estimation (variable time, fixed scope)

evals.name: circuit-breaker-decision
evals.prompt: We're on day 40 of a 6-week Shape Up cycle. The team's bet — a redesigned onboarding flow — isn't done. Two of the four scopes are downhill and shipping in the next few days. The other two scopes are still uphill and the team says they need 'another 2-3 weeks' to finish them well. Leadership is asking whether to extend the cycle or trip the circuit breaker. What should we do?
evals.expected_output: Output should default to the Circuit Breaker (kill, don't extend) rather than the extension. Specifically it should: (a) cite Singer Ch. 14 explicitly — 'Cancel projects that don't ship in one cycle by default instead of extending them by default' and 'If the work is uphill, it's better to do something else in the next cycle and put the troubled project back in the shaping phase'; (b) name that uphill work at the deadline signals a conceptual flaw, not slowness — extension papers over the flaw; (c) suggest shipping the two downhill scopes as scope-cutting-under-appetite (Shape Up's discipline of cutting scope, not extending time); (d) suggest putting the two uphill scopes back into shaping for a future cycle, not carrying them over; (e) name that extension is possible but should be an explicit leadership override, not a default; (f) push back if the user tries to argue 'but we're so close.'
assertions: Output defaults to Circuit Breaker (kill, not extend), not extension
Output cites Singer Ch. 14 or the Circuit Breaker glossary definition with attribution
Output names that uphill work at deadline signals conceptual flaw, not execution slowness
Output suggests shipping the 2 downhill scopes as legitimate scope-cutting to fit appetite
Output suggests putting 2 uphill scopes back into shaping (not carrying over)
Output frames extension as exception (leadership override), not default
Output does NOT endorse extending the cycle as the default response

evals.name: adopt-shape-up-in-non-basecamp-company
evals.prompt: My team is a typical B2B SaaS: 8 engineers (backend and frontend, separate), 2 designers, 3 PMs, QA, separate marketing/sales. We run 2-week Scrum sprints with a JIRA backlog of ~200 tickets. Leadership just read Shape Up and wants to adopt it. Help me think through what's actually realistic. Should we go all-in or borrow specific mechanisms?
evals.expected_output: Output should apply Singer's post-book Shaping in Real Life thinking, not just recite the 2019 book. Specifically it should: (a) name that Basecamp was 'an unusual company' — everyone technical, tiny team, product-led CEO — and adaptation is required; (b) name at least two of the three failure modes from Singer's 2025 Common Pitfalls piece (undershaped work, blurred framing/shaping, mixed reactive work); (c) engineer the technical shaper explicitly — pair non-technical PMs with senior engineers for shaping sessions; (d) address the backlog honestly — 'no backlog' requires CEO commitment, not just a team decision; (e) reference the 2025 End-to-End gym-management case study as a similar-team example; (f) offer honest options — full adoption with leadership sponsorship, or borrowing specific mechanisms (appetite, cool-down, circuit breaker) without the full cadence; (g) NOT sell adoption as easy or promise a frictionless transformation.
assertions: Output names that Basecamp was 'an unusual company' and adaptation is required
Output cites Singer's 2025 Common Pitfalls piece OR names at least 2 of the 3 named failure modes
Output engineers technical shaping explicitly (pair non-technical PMs with senior engineers)
Output addresses the backlog politically (CEO commitment required, not just team decision)
Output references the 2025 gym-management case study OR the Shaping in Real Life material
Output offers a real choice between full adoption and borrowing specific mechanisms
Output does NOT sell adoption as easy or promise frictionless transformation
Output cites at least one specific Singer source (ryansinger.co essay or book chapter URL)

evals.name: framing-vs-shaping-blur
evals.prompt: Great — I'm going to shape a bet on our new mobile checkout flow. The problem is that mobile conversion is 30% lower than desktop. Let me start sketching the solution.
evals.expected_output: Output should pause the user BEFORE shaping and force framing first. Specifically it should: (a) name that 'mobile conversion is 30% lower than desktop' is a metric observation, not a framed problem — is this a problem worth solving 6 weeks on, whose problem is it (small merchants? enterprise? both?), why now, what business value if solved; (b) cite Singer's 2022 Framing essay and the 2025 Common Pitfalls piece on the blurred-framing-and-shaping failure mode; (c) refuse to help sketch a solution until framing produces a framed problem as an artifact; (d) walk the user through the framing questions concretely; (e) NOT proceed to shaping fat-marker sketches just because the user asked for that.
assertions: Output pauses the user BEFORE shaping and forces framing first
Output names that a metric observation ('30% lower conversion') is not a framed problem
Output cites Singer's Framing (2022) essay OR the Common Pitfalls (2025) piece on blurred framing/shaping
Output walks through concrete framing questions (whose problem, why now, business value)
Output does NOT proceed to shaping fat-marker sketches on demand
Output distinguishes 'discussing the problem briefly' from 'framing producing an artifact'

evals.name: shape-up-vs-scrum-choice
evals.prompt: My team runs Scrum. Should we switch to Shape Up? What are the actual tradeoffs?
evals.expected_output: Output should NOT reflexively endorse Shape Up. It should offer a real comparison and identify what makes the switch fit or not fit. Specifically it should: (a) name the core disagreements — backlog vs. no backlog, sprints vs. cycles, estimation vs. appetite, story points vs. fixed time budget; (b) name that Shape Up is defined against Scrum ceremony — blending them collapses the mechanism; (c) name the prerequisites for a successful Shape Up adoption (CEO commitment, post-PMF, teams of enough size, feature bets not maintenance work); (d) offer honest signals of when Scrum is the right tool to keep (need for short feedback loops, backlog is politically load-bearing, small predictable work); (e) offer honest signals of when Shape Up is worth switching to (feature bets with real design surface, willing to commit to no backlog, willing to default-kill); (f) NOT sell Shape Up as universally better; (g) reference the applications.md-style comparison if possible.
assertions: Output does NOT reflexively endorse Shape Up over Scrum
Output names the core disagreements (backlog, sprints vs cycles, estimation vs appetite)
Output names that blending Shape Up and Scrum collapses the mechanism
Output names prerequisites for Shape Up adoption (CEO commitment, post-PMF, team size, feature bets only)
Output offers honest signals for when Scrum is the right tool to keep
Output offers honest signals for when Shape Up is worth adopting
Output cites Singer or the book at least once
Output tone is measured and dispositional (matches Singer's voice, not polemical)
